title: Raman and SEM Enabled Development of Natural Organic Fructose Thin Films for Resistive Switching Memory in Neuromorphic Computing Applications
content: Fructose, abundant in natural sources such as fruits and vegetables, is one of the three dietary monosaccharides, along with glucose and galactose. Recently, fructose has been investigated [1] as a promising natural organic material for use as a dielectric film in environmentally friendly electronic devices, addressing the global e-waste issue. In this study, we report on the microscopy, spectroscopy, and electrical characterization of fructose films developed as active resistive layers in resistive switching random access memory (ReRAM) devices, a critical component for neuromorphic computing systems. The fructose films were fabricated via a solution-based process, using spin-coating of a 0.7 M fructose-water solution on an ITO substrate as the bottom electrode, followed by annealing at 80°C for varying durations. A patterned aluminum film was deposited on top as the top electrode. Fig. 1(a)-(e) illustrates the fabrication process of the fructose thin film and ReRAM devices. The annealing time plays a critical role in the formation of the fructose thin film. Fig. 2(a) presents an SEM image of the film surface annealed at 80°C for 6 hours, which is considered optimal for film development. Raman spectra of the films annealed for different durations are shown in Fig. 1(b). The 6-hour annealing duration yields the best overall quality, improving crystallinity and reducing hydration compared to the 4-hour and 8-hour anneals. These findings align with the SEM image in Fig. 1(b), where the 6-hour annealed film exhibits a smooth, even surface. The Raman spectra also suggest that due to the film's thin (∼100 nm) nature, the substrate dominates the spectrum below ∼1400 cm-1. However, two prominent peaks at 1460 cm-1 and 2946 cm-1 (with a shoulder at 2905 cm-1) decrease with longer annealing times, indicating increasing amorphization, consistent with previous reports [2]. The 1460 cm-1 peak correlates with water content reduction, while the 2946 cm-1 peak, linked to C-H and -CH2 stretching, diminishes as crystallinity decreases.
